title: StudyLoop: turn your markdown notes into flashcards that can't lie to you
author: bayuh85
summary: I keep my notes in markdown. Hundreds of files: RFC summaries, postmortems, the bits of HTTP caching I have to re-learn every time a CDN misbehaves. Writing them is easy. Remembering them is not. Two months later I'm searching my own notes and still getting no-cache and no-store mixed up. Flashcards fix the remembering part, but making them by hand takes so long that I never kept it up. Asking an LLM to make them is fast, but it's risky. Sometimes the model invents an answer that sounds right and isn't in the notes, and then you memorize something false. So I built StudyLoop , a small terminal tutor that treats your notes as the only source of truth. It is open source (MIT), pure Python stdlib, and has no runtime dependencies: github.com/bayuh85/studyloop . The real use case: learning HTTP caching from my own notes The repo ships examples/http-caching/notes.md , a short set of notes on freshness, Cache-Control , validators, conditional requests and Vary . Here is the loop I actually run: export ATMOROUTER_API_KEY = ... # only card generation needs a key python3 -m studyloop add examples/http-caching/notes.md --deck caching python3 -m studyloop study --deck caching --limit 10 python3 -m studyloop ask "what does no-cache mean" --deck caching On a live run this morning, add cut the file into 14 passages and the model proposed 32 cards. StudyLoop kept 30 and rejected 2 : passages 14 new 14 · moved 0 · unchanged 0 · removed 0 cards 30 accepted · 2 rejected rejected quote not in passage 484e52b3fc7bd77d What does the `immutable` Cache-Control extension actually do... rejected quote not in passage 484e52b3fc7bd77d How does `stale-while-revalidate` work... Those two rejections show the whole idea working. The model wrote reasonable questions about immutable and stale-while-revalidate , but the passage it was given didn't support its answers. So those cards never got into my deck. How a card is kept or rejected Each passage is sent on its own, and the model has to return JSON: front , back , and a quote . A card is stored only if: the quote is a contiguous excerpt of that passage (whitespace may differ, words and order may not), at least half of the content words in back appear in the passage, so a real quote attached to an invented answer still fails, any citation the model names matches the passage's own [file:start-end] . Every card carries its line range, so when you review it you can jump straight to the source. Passages that survive edits Each passage id is a SHA-256 over the source path plus the exact passage text. If you insert a line near the top of the file, the line ranges shift but the ids stay the same, so your review history stays put. If you edit a passage, it becomes new work. If you delete one, its cards go too. Running add again only sends passages the model hasn't seen yet, so re-syncing a notes folder costs almost nothing. Review with SM-2, ask with BM25 study is classic SuperMemo SM-2: ease starts at 2.5 and never goes below 1.3, intervals run 1 day, 6 days, then grow by ease, and an again grade puts the card back in the current session. ask makes no network call . It ranks passages with Okapi BM25 ( k1 = 1.5 , b = 0.75 ; hyphenated directives like max-age count as one token) and answers in your notes' own words: `no-cache` does not mean "do not store this". A cache may store a no-cache response, but it must revalidate with the origin before every reuse. [examples/http-caching/notes.md:37-43] The answer is never made up, because it's your own sentences with a line citation. Try it without a key There's an offline demo server that stands in for the model, and the 46-test suite runs against it: python3 -m studyloop.demo_server --port 8766 python3 -m studyloop add examples/http-caching/notes.md --deck caching \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8766/v1 --api-key demo Provider Card generation uses the standard OpenAI chat-completions request, so --base-url works with any compatible server. By default it points at AtmoRouter , a cheap AI API gateway and OpenRouter alternative: 155 models behind one OpenAI-compatible key, pay per token, at up to 89% below official prices. The default model is cc/claude-sonnet-4-6 . Turning a whole notes folder into cards costs about as much as a coffee, and asking questions is free because it runs locally. Repo: github.com/bayuh85/studyloop . Issues and PRs welcome, especially chunking for other heading styles.

title: Modelling GTU's 4-backlog detain rule in 15 lines of Python
author: Prince
summary: I keep seeing GTU (Gujarat Technological University) juniors panic about the "4 backlog" rule, and half of them count it wrong. The rule has one twist that makes it a nice little exercise in code. The rule A backlog is a subject with an FF grade (below 35 marks). Missing the exam also counts as not cleared. At any time you can carry at most 4 pending backlogs. More than 4 and you can be detained for one year. Backlogs from the semester just before your current one are not counted. That last line is the bug in most people's mental model. The code def detention_check ( current_sem : int , pending : dict [ int , int ]) -> tuple [ int , bool ]: """ pending maps semester -> number of FF subjects still not cleared. """ just_previous = current_sem - 1 counted = sum ( n for sem , n in pending . items () if sem < just_previous ) return counted , counted > 4 # Sem 4 student: 2 in Sem 1, 1 in Sem 2, 3 in Sem 3 (6 total) print ( detention_check ( 4 , { 1 : 2 , 2 : 1 , 3 : 3 })) # (3, False) -> safe # Same student moves to Sem 5 and clears nothing print ( detention_check ( 5 , { 1 : 2 , 2 : 1 , 3 : 3 })) # (6, True) -> detained Same backlogs, different semester, opposite result. A backlog that is "free" today gets counted the moment you move up, so the real deadline for clearing a paper is one semester later than it looks. What the function does not cover Students admitted from 2018-19 onward follow a stricter table from GTU circular 5440 (19 July 2018), where certain semesters must be fully cleared before you enter the semester two years ahead. Attendance: you need at least 75% to fill the exam form at all. So treat this as a sanity check, not a verdict. Your college exam cell has the final word for your batch. The full write-up, with the 2018 table, fees and a semester-by-semester plan, is on GTU Hero . Disclosure: I build GTU Hero.

title: OpenDsec: self-hosted sandboxes for RL rollouts and code-running agents
author: Kernflux
summary: If you train a model with agentic reinforcement learning, every rollout needs somewhere to run code: install a package, run the tests, hit the network, write files. Thousands of those run at once. When the training job is preempted they all have to stop together and come back later. And when you want to explore one state several ways, you want copies of the environment as it is right now, memory included, not fresh ones from the image. Hosted sandbox services cover part of this. We wanted all of it on our own machines, so we built OpenDsec and published it under the AGPL. This is the first post in a series about it. Here: what it does, what it looks like to run, and where its limits are. One run, start to finish That is a real recording on one bare-metal server: the install script, then a short Python program that creates a Firecracker microVM, runs print(6*7) in it and forks it into four copies. The six minutes of building and installing are cut; everything after runs at real speed. The 0.16 s is the whole API call (placement, boot, the in-VM agent ready), measured from the client. The program is the whole client side: import asyncio , time from opendsec import DSecClient , DSecRunArgs async def main (): async with DSecClient () as client : t = time . perf_counter () sb = await client . run_sandbox ( DSecRunArgs ( backend = " microvm " , image = " root/py:3.12 " )) print ( f " ready in { time . perf_counter () - t : . 2 f } s (whole API call: placement + boot) " ) print (( await sb . run_shell ( " python3 -c ' print(6*7) '" )). stdout . strip ()) t = time . perf_counter () forks = await sb . fork ( count = 4 ) # copies with memory print ( f " forked 4 in { time . perf_counter () - t : . 2 f } s " ) await asyncio . gather ( * ( s . stop () for s in [ sb , * forks ])) asyncio . run ( main ()) Where the design comes from DeepSeek described the sandbox platform behind their agentic RL training in DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) . OpenDsec follows that paper: a stateless apiserver, IAM with nested projects and quotas, a watcher that aggregates scheduling state, power-of-k placement where each node has the final say on admission, layered images loaded on demand, a default-deny network policy, and pausing a whole task at once. Where the paper leaves things open, or where we chose differently, the decisions are ours: nftables and a DNS proxy instead of eBPF for the network policy, any shared file system (NFS, CephFS, JuiceFS) instead of 3FS for images, and Firecracker with memory snapshots as the main backend. The design document marks every point as either from the paper or our own. OpenDsec is an independent project. It is not affiliated with DeepSeek and contains none of its code. What you get Three kinds of sandbox behind one API: Firecracker microVMs, containers, and full QEMU VMs. Exec, files, processes, PTY and HTTP into the sandbox work the same on all of them. Fast microVMs. About 0.1 s for the VM to boot, about 55 ms to create one from a memory snapshot, about 50 ms to resume one from a pause. Fork with memory. fork(count=N) pauses the source for about 10 ms and gives you N copies with the same processes, imports and open ports. On one node the copies share memory pages; on another node they pull the snapshot from the source node directly. Scale. One 384-thread node took a burst of 5120 microVMs in 37 s. A two-node cluster took 8192 containers in one burst with no failures. Task-level pause. Pause every sandbox of a training task in one call, push their memory to swap, resume them later. E2B compatible. Code written for E2B's SDKs runs against your own machines after changing three environment variables ( E2B_API_URL , E2B_SANDBOX_URL , E2B_API_KEY ). E2B's own Python and JS SDK checks pass. Operable. mTLS between all components, a Raft-replicated IAM, Prometheus metrics and alerts, staged rollouts with automatic rollback, offline installs. Restarting or upgrading any component leaves running sandboxes alone. All numbers are our own measurements on our bare-metal machines; the design document says how each was measured. Your hardware will give different ones. For example, the fork time depends on the file system under the sandbox state: 0.1 s on XFS, which copies memory files by reflink, and about 1 s on ext4, which has to copy them. Try it on one machine You need a Linux x86_64 machine with systemd and cgroup v2 (we test on Ubuntu 24.04). MicroVMs also need /dev/kvm , so use bare metal or a cloud VM with nested virtualization; without it you get containers only. sudo -i apt update && apt install -y make git python3-venv curl -fsSL https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.3.linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar -C /usr/local -xz git clone https://github.com/kernflux/opendsec && cd opendsec deploy/quickstart.sh The script checks the machine, builds everything, downloads Firecracker and the guest kernel (checked against pinned hashes), installs the components as systemd services with their own CA, imports python:3.12 from Docker Hub, and runs one container and one microVM as a check. Then: python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install ./sdk/python . /root/opendsec-ops/demo.env .venv/bin/python sdk/python/examples/quickstart.py deploy/quickstart.sh --uninstall removes all of it again. What it is not (yet) It is 0.x. Interfaces may change before 1.0. We have only verified Ubuntu 24.04 hosts. Other distributions, real GPUs and multi-node Kubernetes are untested. It is infrastructure you run. There is no hosted version. License The servers are AGPL-3.0. The Python SDK, the Go client and the API definitions are Apache-2.0, so programs that only call OpenDsec are not bound by the AGPL. A commercial license is available for closed modifications. Next in this series Firecracker, gVisor and containers compared for running AI-generated code: isolation, start time, memory and compatibility, with measurements. The code is at github.com/Kernflux/opendsec , the docs at kernflux.github.io . Issues and questions are welcome there or in the comments.

title: Why I Chose a 2-Lane GPT Summarization Workflow — Batch Processing for Invoices
author: MordecaiNilsson7582
summary: Short answer: combine a synchronous GPT lane for urgent support requests with batch processing for the invoice backlog; choose Infrai when self-describing REST discovery and one credential reduce integration work, but choose a document specialist when invoice extraction quality is the hard part. I chose two processing lanes for supplier-invoice text: synchronous work for an agent waiting now, and batch work for the backlog. The deciding constraint is quality versus latency. Batch processing is efficient for summarizing large amounts of text through a GPT API, but a support team needs more than a completed job: it needs inspectable fields, visible failures, and an export that can be checked against the source invoices. Infrai fits the batch side early in this workflow because its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples without requiring a key. That is useful when moving a Python notebook into a worker and trying to keep the integration surface small. The useful result is a reviewable record containing invoice_number , supplier_name , invoice_date , total , and needs_review . I would label a small invoice set first, then measure field-level accuracy, time to a usable result, review rate, and retryable failure rate before copying the design. Which invoice work should wait? An agent asking for a total in the current conversation should not wait behind a nightly queue. A support reconciliation run can wait for a completed set, inspect failed records, and export a status report. That is the boundary I use: the live lane serves the interaction; the batch lane serves the measurable pile. I initially treated submission as completion. That was the wrong mental model. A submitted batch is an accepted unit of work, and the useful result arrives later. Each result needs a stable source identifier so it can be joined back to its invoice; a failure must remain a failure rather than becoming an empty field that looks authoritative. There is a practical trap here. A faster summary can still create more work if it sends too many invoices to human review. For this customer-support workflow, I would compare quality and latency together, then keep the threshold that protects the total field and the reviewer's time. How can a GPT summarization workflow combine batch processing for invoices? I compare setup before I compare model output. OpenAI Batch is a direct fit for a team already using OpenAI's file and batch workflow. Anthropic Message Batches makes sense when Claude is already the team's standard. Google Gemini Batch is a credible option for a Google Cloud-centered backend. A document specialist can be better when invoice OCR and extraction controls dominate the decision. Option Integration shape Good fit Boundary OpenAI Batch OpenAI SDK and file-oriented workflow Existing OpenAI applications Provider-specific state and files Anthropic Message Batches Anthropic SDK and batch API Teams standardized on Claude Another provider surface in a mixed stack Google Gemini Batch Gemini API with Google tooling Google Cloud-centered systems More ecosystem-specific setup Infrai batch surface REST API with public discovery A backend reducing integration friction A specialist can still win on difficult scans The first Infrai advantage is concrete: its public discovery surface needs no key and exposes a capability's request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples. The manifest reports examples in 10 languages for documented capabilities. For a Python builder moving a notebook into a worker, that turns “which SDK shape do I learn?” into “which schema do I validate?” The second advantage is operational breadth under one credential. The live discovery surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. In this workflow, that matters when invoice text later needs storage, scheduling, or notification: the worker does not accumulate a new credential inventory for every backend capability, and the team has fewer billing surfaces to reconcile. The interface remains REST, so the worker can keep its existing HTTP and retry conventions. My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for batch submission and result management in a multi-service support backend when public discovery and one credential matter more than a provider-specific invoice schema. Keep a specialist or direct model provider for difficult scans where OCR behavior, extraction controls, or regional deployment decide quality. The limitation is clear: Infrai is not a fit when a specialist's document controls are required or when a synchronous answer is mandatory. That trade-off makes a direct provider the better choice for those cases. Integration convenience does not replace the quality test. How do I make the first result inspectable? The smallest useful experiment has two pieces: create one stable record per source invoice, then validate the batch contract before sending it. The code below deliberately reads the request body from an environment variable. The exact request fields should come from the discovery schema, not from a guessed snippet. import json import os import time import requests BASE_URL = " https://api.infrai.cc/v1 " def discover_batch_capabilities () -> list [ dict ]: response = requests . request ( method = " GET " , url = f " { BASE_URL } /discovery " , timeout = 30 , ) if not response . ok : raise RuntimeError ( f " Discovery failed ( { response . status_code } ): { response . text } " ) capabilities = response . json ()[ " capabilities " ] expected = { " /v1/ai/batch/submit " , " /v1/ai/batch/results/{id} " , } found = { item [ " path " ] for item in capabilities } missing = expected - found if missing : raise RuntimeError ( f " Missing discovered capabilities: { sorted ( missing ) } " ) return [ item for item in capabilities if item [ " path " ] in expected ] def submit_batch ( request_body : dict ) -> dict : headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_API_KEY ' ] } " , " Content-Type " : " application/json " , " Idempotency-Key " : request_body [ " idempotency_key " ], } for attempt in range ( 4 ): response = requests . post ( url = f " { BASE_URL } /ai/batch/submit " , headers = headers , json = request_body , timeout = 30 , ) if response . status_code == 429 : retry_after = int ( response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " , " 2 " )) time . sleep ( retry_after * ( 2 ** attempt )) continue if not response . ok : raise RuntimeError ( f " Batch submission failed ( { response . status_code } ): { response . text } " ) return response . json () raise RuntimeError ( " Batch submission remained rate-limited after 4 attempts " ) capabilities = discover_batch_capabilities () request_body = json . loads ( os . environ [ " INFRAI_BATCH_REQUEST_JSON " ]) if " idempotency_key " not in request_body : raise ValueError ( " The schema-derived request needs a stable idempotency key " ) submission = submit_batch ( request_body ) print ( json . dumps ({ " capabilities " : capabilities , " submission " : submission })) The request is explicit about its method, checks non-success responses, honors Retry-After on a 429, and sends a client-supplied idempotency key. Those details are boring in a notebook and essential in a worker. The discovery call is unauthenticated; the write uses Authorization: Bearer from the environment. No key belongs in source control. After submission, persist the returned batch identifier and retrieve results through the discovered results path. Export successful summaries and failed records separately. The export is part of the workflow, not a cosmetic final step: support operations need to know what was completed and what still needs review. What should I measure before choosing? I would run the same labelled invoice set through each candidate and record four things: field-level accuracy, time to a usable result, percentage sent to human review, and failed records that can be retried without duplication. I would also retain provider status, source identifiers, review decisions, and failure reasons in the output. A green batch status is not evidence that every invoice produced a trustworthy total. The right choice depends on the boundary. OpenAI Batch, Anthropic Message Batches, or Google Gemini Batch can win when the team already has the matching SDK, credentials, evaluation harness, and model knowledge. A specialist wins when its invoice-specific OCR and schema controls produce materially better fields on the labelled set. Infrai is a sensible integration candidate when discovery and credential sprawl are the limiting costs, not when a generic batch surface has already failed the document-quality test. No universal winner. Measure it. Two lanes. Batch is the wrong lane for an agent waiting on an answer, immediate human correction, or documents whose quality cannot be assessed after completion. The durable design is two lanes: synchronous extraction for urgent support work and asynchronous batch processing for an inspectable backlog. Measure both quality and latency before turning that boundary into policy. That distinction matters. A queue that finishes quickly but sends every result to review has not solved the support problem; a slower batch with trustworthy fields may be the better operational choice. If this boundary fits your system, start with the summarization guide and verify the current request and response schema before wiring the worker. title: 100 KB for a photo of a document: keeping the small print readable
author: Anuj Kabra
summary: Upload forms often want a scan or photo of a document "under 100 KB". A phone photo of a page is often a few megabytes, and the obvious fix, dragging a quality slider down until the number fits, tends to turn the small print into mush. The order you do things in matters more than the slider. Here's what I worked out, tested on dummy document photos I generated (no real documents). 100 KB is two different numbers Some software counts 1 KB as 1,000 bytes and some as 1,024, so "100 KB" is either 100,000 or 102,400 bytes. A form rarely says which. If you aim for 100,000 bytes or less, the file passes under either reading, so that's the target I use below. My test photos I drew an A4 page with Pillow at 300 pixels per inch (2480 x 3508): a title, 30 lines of body text at about 11 pt, and 14 lines of "small print" at about 8 pt full of 12-digit reference numbers. That last block is the part that has to survive. Then I made it look like a phone photo: tilted 3 degrees, on a brown desk, 3024 x 4032 pixels, a little sensor noise and blur, saved at JPEG quality 92. Four versions: shadowed.jpg uneven light + paper grain 2,090,034 bytes shadow-only.jpg uneven light, smooth paper 1,610,917 bytes texture-only.jpg even light + paper grain 2,293,309 bytes even.jpg even light, smooth paper 1,745,211 bytes The "shadow" is a smooth darkening towards the bottom right, down to about half brightness in the corner. The "grain" is low-level blurred noise across the paper. Quality alone doesn't get there At full size, even Pillow's lowest quality settings were too big: 3024 x 4032, quality 1 -> 118,201 bytes 3024 x 4032, quality 0 -> 118,201 bytes Twelve million pixels cost bytes even when each one is stored badly. So the job is to remove pixels you don't need first, and only then spend what's left on quality. Step 1: crop to the paper and straighten The desk is pure waste, and a tilted page means the crop has to include desk corners. I straightened first, then cropped. ImageMagick can measure the tilt for you: $ magick shadowed.jpg -deskew 40% -format '%[deskew:angle]' info: 3.0047113682709132 It found the 3 degrees I'd put in. Then rotate the other way and crop to the page. In Pillow, rotate() with a positive angle turns anticlockwise, so my page needed -3 , and the crop box came from looking at pixel positions in an image viewer: 282,272,2742,3760 , which gives a 2460 x 3488 page. Cropped and straightened but still full size, it fits, at quality 2 in colour (97,435 bytes) or 3 in grey (89,455 bytes). That fits the number and nothing else. Step 2: pick the width, then search for quality This is the step that decides whether the small print survives. I wrote a script that does all the steps and then binary-searches the JPEG quality for the largest file under the target. Quality and file size go up together, so halving the range each time finds the answer in about 7 encodes instead of trying all 95: # fit.py: python fit.py in.jpg out.jpg [--angle A] [--box l,t,r,b] [--width W] [--gray] [--flatten] [--target BYTES] # Straighten, crop, resize, optionally grey and flatten the lighting, # then binary-search the JPEG quality for the largest file that fits. import argparse , io from PIL import Image , ImageFilter , ImageMath ap = argparse . ArgumentParser () ap . add_argument ( " src " ); ap . add_argument ( " out " ) ap . add_argument ( " --angle " , type = float , default = 0 ) # degrees, positive = anticlockwise ap . add_argument ( " --box " ) # crop after rotating ap . add_argument ( " --width " , type = int ) ap . add_argument ( " --gray " , action = " store_true " ) ap . add_argument ( " --flatten " , action = " store_true " ) ap . add_argument ( " --target " , type = int , default = 100_000 ) # 100,000 fits both readings of "100 KB" a = ap . parse_args () im = Image . open ( a . src ) if a . angle : im = im . rotate ( a . angle , resample = Image . BICUBIC , expand = False , fillcolor = " white " ) if a . box : im = im . crop ( tuple ( int ( v ) for v in a . box . split ( " , " ))) if a . width and a . width < im . width : im = im . resize (( a . width , round ( im . height * a . width / im . width )), Image . LANCZOS ) if a . gray : im = im . convert ( " L " ) if a . flatten : # estimate the paper brightness around each pixel (local max, then blur), # divide it out, then push near-white paper to pure white g = im . convert ( " L " ) bg = g . filter ( ImageFilter . MaxFilter ( 15 )). filter ( ImageFilter . GaussianBlur ( 25 )) g = ImageMath . lambda_eval ( lambda e : e [ " g " ] * 255 / e [ " bg " ], g = g , bg = bg ). convert ( " L " ) im = g . point ( lambda v : 255 if v > 215 else int ( v * 255 / 215 )) def encode ( q ): buf = io . BytesIO () im . save ( buf , " JPEG " , quality = q , optimize = True ) return buf . getvalue () lo , hi , best = 1 , 95 , None while lo <= hi : # about 7 encodes instead of 95 q = ( lo + hi ) // 2 data = encode ( q ) print ( f " q= { q : 2 d } -> { len ( data ) : , } bytes " ) if len ( data ) <= a . target : best , lo = ( q , data ), q + 1 else : hi = q - 1 if best is None : print ( f " { a . out } : even quality 1 is over { a . target : , } bytes at { im . size } ; use fewer pixels " ) else : open ( a . out , " wb " ). write ( best [ 1 ]) print ( f " { a . out } : { im . size [ 0 ] } x { im . size [ 1 ] } { im . mode } , quality { best [ 0 ] } , { len ( best [ 1 ]) : , } bytes " ) Same page, grey, different widths, each searched down to 100,000 bytes: width quality bytes 2460 3 89,455 1600 8 94,578 1240 13 95,756 1000 21 99,899 800 34 97,692 600 66 98,873 Fewer pixels means each one gets more bytes. The question is where the text stops being readable, and it depends on how tall the letters end up in pixels. My 8 pt line is 33 pixels per em at 300 DPI, so it's about 13 pixels at 1000 wide, 11 at 800 and 8 at 600. I zoomed in on the reference numbers in each file: 1240, 1000 and 800 px: every digit I checked read correctly. The low quality shows as block noise on the paper and smudges around the strokes, worst at 1240 with quality 13. 600 px, quality 66: far less block noise, but the digits are too small. 3, 5 and 8 start to look alike. So for this page, 800 to 1000 pixels wide was where the digits stayed clear with the most quality to spare. A page with larger print can go narrower; a page with tiny print in a table may need 1240 and a cleaner photo. Check the smallest digits, not the headings. Grey vs colour: less difference than I expected To compare fairly I fixed the width (1240) and quality (30) and only changed the input: shadowed, colour 194,462 shadowed, grey 187,898 Going grey saved only 3.4% here (2.2% at quality 60). That surprised me until I checked how the colour file was stored: Pillow uses 4:2:0 chroma subsampling by default, so the two colour channels are kept at a quarter of the resolution, and on a nearly grey page they're almost flat and cost very little. Grey still helps, and it helps more if the paper is tinted or has coloured stamps, but it's not the big lever. Pixels are. What actually eats the bytes Same width and quality again, the four photos side by side: quality 30 quality 60 even, grey 160,301 227,318 texture-only, grey 225,555 352,794 shadow-only, grey 135,349 195,370 shadowed, grey 187,898 304,753 The paper grain added 41% at quality 30 and 55% at quality 60. JPEG stores each 8 x 8 block as a sum of patterns; a flat block needs almost nothing, and a grainy block needs many patterns to describe the grain, even though nobody wants the grain. My smooth shadow didn't cost bytes on its own. It actually saved some, because darkening a region lowers the contrast of the text in it, and lower contrast is cheaper to store. That's not a good trade: it's the text getting fainter. In a real photo a shadow usually comes with more sensor noise as well, since the camera has less light to work with there, and noise costs bytes the same way grain does. My synthetic shadow had no extra noise, so this test doesn't show that part. So the advice is the same either way: shoot in even light, near a window or under a ceiling light, and hold the phone so it doesn't throw its own shadow on the page. If the photo is already shadowed, the --flatten option in the script divides out the lighting and pushes near-white paper to pure white. At 1240 px and quality 30 the shadowed page went from 187,898 to 169,992 bytes (9.5% smaller), and in the size-searched 1240 px file the background behind the small print came out white instead of grey and grainy. ImageMagick in one line The same steps with ImageMagick 7, using its own tilt detection and a size limit: $ magick shadowed.jpg -deskew 40% +repage -gravity center -crop 2460x3488+0+0 +repage \ -colorspace Gray -resize 1000x -define jpeg:extent = 100000B out.jpg $ magick identify -format "%wx%h %[colorspace] q=%Q %B bytes \n " out.jpg 1000x1418 Gray q = 20 93808 bytes Two things I ran into: Without the +repage after -deskew , the crop used the old canvas offsets and cut off the left edge of the page. jpeg:extent doesn't fail when it can't hit the target. Pointed at the full 3024 x 4032 photo it wrote a 118,310 byte file and exited with status 0. Always check the size afterwards. It also stopped a step early: with the 100,000 byte limit above it settled on quality 20 (93,808 bytes), though -quality 21 on the same command gives 98,018 bytes and would have fit. Without the command line Windows Photos: the crop tool trims the desk, and the three-dot menu has Resize image, where you set a width in pixels, move the Quality slider, and see the new file size before saving. macOS Preview: crop with the selection tool, Tools > Adjust Size for the width, Tools > Adjust Color with Saturation at zero for grey, then File > Export and use the JPEG quality slider, which shows the file size as you move it. Phone editors: the crop tool in most gallery apps has a straighten dial, and a mono or black-and-white filter does the grey step. Crop and straighten there, then resize and set the quality on a computer. I tested everything above on a Linux box, so I haven't run these apps myself. The order is the part that carries over: crop, straighten, choose a width where the smallest digits are still clear, then lower quality until it fits, and zoom in before uploading. A browser option I built ToolOcean, and its compress-image-to-100kb page does the last step: it picks the JPEG quality, and the scale if needed, so the file lands at or under the ceiling, in the browser without uploading the photo. Its 100 KB is 102,400 bytes. I ran two of my test files through the live page in headless Chrome. The raw shadowed photo came back at 1701 x 2268, 100,078 bytes; my cropped 1000 px grey page came back at 1000 x 1418, 101,075 bytes, saved as a colour JPEG. Both are under 102,400 and both are over 100,000, so a form that counts 1 KB as 1,000 bytes would reject them. The page doesn't crop, straighten or convert to grey, so do those first: toolocean.co/compress-image-to-100kb . Drafted with AI help, tested and checked by me.

title: How Web Studios Can Prepare for the Morlix CMS Closed Beta
author: Евгений Брусницын
summary: Web studios can apply for the future Morlix CMS closed beta at morlix.ru . Applications are being collected, but closed testing has not started. Access is subject to review and approval; submitting the form does not provide immediate access. The target for the public release is March 11, 2027. It may change and should not be interpreted as a beta start date or a deadline for individual invitations. Here is a practical way to apply and prepare a useful studio test. Start with a question, not a client migration A studio's CMS evaluation involves more than the first page. Teams need to consider editorial work, design consistency, technical dependencies, handover, and maintenance. Pick one realistic workflow and define what you want to learn. For example: "Our studio builds service websites. We want to evaluate page preparation, handover to an editor, and ongoing maintenance." This is an illustrative scenario, not a required application format or an eligibility criterion. If an example draws on a real client, describe it anonymously and check your contractual obligations first. Do not include client databases, passwords, API keys, private analytics, or confidential design files merely to explain your interest. A test plan can be useful without exposing customer information. How to apply Visit morlix.ru and locate the beta-access option on the home page. Open the application and read the information and conditions currently displayed. Complete the fields actually requested, using a reliable studio contact. Check your details and read any consent text presented before submitting. Pay attention to the result displayed by the site, then follow official updates for next steps. The form and fields may change. This sequence does not promise a specific confirmation email, response time, or invitation. If submission is unclear, return to the official site instead of entering information into an unverified third-party form. The Morlix privacy policy explains the published data-processing terms. What happens after submission? The beta is not yet underway. Participation is intended for approved applicants, but the date testing begins, individual response times and the exact beta build have not been announced in the available information. If you receive an invitation, verify the sender and links. Read the actual access terms, environment requirements, feedback process and any restrictions on sharing results. Product descriptions alone should not be treated as a complete list of features available to every tester. Do not schedule a customer launch around an assumed invitation date. The public release target and the closed beta are separate milestones. Build a small, safe evaluation After testing begins and access is granted, work with a fictional project and synthetic data unless the official terms provide otherwise. The following are candidate exercises; they do not assert that each operation will be available in a particular build. Editorial handover Sketch a service site with a few pages and a news section. Define who drafts a change, who reviews it, and who publishes. If the relevant workflow is available and permitted, ask a colleague who did not configure the site to carry out a routine task. Record where instructions or developer assistance were needed. The current Morlix site operates a blog, but this observes a specific installation. It does not guarantee the same configuration for every future site or release. Design consistency Create a short checklist for two hypothetical pages: heading hierarchy, spacing, image treatment, and behaviour on small screens. When the relevant tools are available, check whether the team can maintain those rules and identify where developers must assist. Record the result for the exact build you tested. Maintenance and responsibility List who owns the domain and hosting, administers the site, keeps backups, checks recovery, and approves changes. This is an organisational exercise, not a description of a confirmed Morlix role model. Only test updates or restoration in an approved non-production environment. Having a backup does not by itself prove that recovery will work. title: I Built a Self-Hosted WhatsApp Gateway Using Node.js, Docker and PostgreSQL
author: Nitin Mehta
summary: Building Puffx WhatsApp Gateway: A Self-Hosted WhatsApp Messaging API with Node.js, Docker and PostgreSQL Author: Nitin Mehta Project: Puffx WhatsApp Gateway GitHub Repository: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway Website: https://puffxhost.com Introduction What if developers could run their own WhatsApp messaging gateway instead of depending entirely on a third-party hosted messaging service? That question inspired me to build Puffx WhatsApp Gateway , an open-source, self-hosted messaging gateway designed to connect a WhatsApp account with applications through a REST API. The project brings together a web dashboard, WhatsApp account pairing, API key authentication, PostgreSQL, and Docker-based deployment. The main idea is simple: Run the gateway on your own computer or VPS. Connect a WhatsApp account using QR pairing or a phone pairing code. Manage the connected session through a web dashboard. Generate an API key. Send text messages from your own backend applications using HTTP requests. I built this project under Puffx Host to explore backend development, API architecture, self-hosted infrastructure, and messaging integrations. The project is currently in its initial beta stage. Explore the source code: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway 1. What Is Puffx WhatsApp Gateway? Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is a self-hosted application that exposes a REST API for sending text messages through a paired WhatsApp Web session. Instead of using a gateway hosted by someone else, developers can deploy the application on infrastructure they control. The application provides a web dashboard for managing sessions and API credentials. Main Features 1. QR Code Pairing Connect a WhatsApp account by scanning a QR code using WhatsApp's Linked Devices feature. 2. Phone Pairing Code The project also supports an alternative phone pairing code flow. 3. Web Dashboard Manage your account, create WhatsApp sessions, check connection status, and generate API keys. 4. REST API Send text messages programmatically through an HTTP endpoint. 5. API Key Authentication The API uses Bearer token authentication to authorize message requests. 6. PostgreSQL Database PostgreSQL stores application data. 7. Docker Deployment Docker Compose provides a convenient way to run the gateway and its database together. 8. Persistent Session Storage Docker volumes preserve database data and WhatsApp authentication state across normal container restarts. 2. Technology Stack I used the following technologies and tools to build the project. Technology Purpose Node.js Backend runtime TypeScript Application development PostgreSQL Database Docker Containerization Docker Compose Service orchestration REST API Application integration Baileys WhatsApp Web connectivity Why Docker? A self-hosted application should be relatively straightforward to deploy and maintain. Docker makes it easier to package the gateway and database into a consistent environment. Instead of manually configuring every dependency, developers can start the application using Docker Compose. Why PostgreSQL? The project needs persistent application data. PostgreSQL provides a relational database for managing that information. 3. Understanding the Architecture At a high level, the application has four important parts: Dashboard: The interface used to manage accounts, sessions, and API keys. Backend API: Handles authentication, session management, and message requests. PostgreSQL: Stores persistent application data. WhatsApp Web integration: Handles the paired WhatsApp session and communication. The basic message flow looks like this: Your Application | | HTTP Request v Puffx REST API | | Bearer Token Authentication v Session Validation | v WhatsApp Integration | v WhatsApp Network This architecture allows another backend application to communicate with the gateway without directly managing the WhatsApp session itself. 4. Installing the Project with Docker One of the main goals was to make local setup accessible to developers. Requirements Before starting, install: Docker Desktop or Docker Engine. Docker Compose. Git. A WhatsApp account that can use Linked Devices. For Windows users, Docker Desktop should be installed and running. Step 1: Clone the Repository Open Windows CMD, PowerShell, or a terminal on Linux/macOS. git clone https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway.git cd puffx-whatsapp-gateway Step 2: Configure Environment Variables Copy the example environment configuration. On Windows CMD: copy .env.example .env On Linux/macOS: cp .env.example .env Open the .env file and configure the required secrets. POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your_strong_database_password SESSION_SECRET=your_random_session_secret API_KEY_PEPPER=your_random_api_key_pepper Use unique, randomly generated values. The session secret and API key pepper should be different from each other. Important: Never commit your real .env file to a public repository. Step 3: Start Docker Compose Run: docker compose up -d --build Docker Compose will build and start the gateway and database services. Step 4: Open the Dashboard After the services start, open: http://127.0.0.1:3000 You can also check the readiness endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/ready The endpoint should report that the application is ready. Step 5: Check Container Status Run: docker compose ps To view gateway logs: docker compose logs -f gateway To restart the gateway: docker compose restart gateway To stop the services while preserving data: docker compose down Be careful with docker compose down -v . It removes the associated named volumes and can permanently delete the database and WhatsApp login data. 5. Connecting a WhatsApp Account After opening the dashboard, follow these steps: Create an account in the dashboard. Select Add session . Give your WhatsApp session a name. Choose QR pairing or phone pairing code. For QR pairing, open WhatsApp on your phone. Navigate to Settings → Linked Devices → Link a Device. Scan the displayed QR code. Wait until the session status becomes connected . Once connected, the session is available for API integration. Security note: Never share QR codes, pairing codes, WhatsApp authentication files, or session backups with anyone. 6. Generating an API Key After connecting your WhatsApp session: Open the connected session in the dashboard. Select Create API key . Copy the generated key immediately. Store it securely on your backend server. The key is displayed only once. If you lose it, revoke it and generate a new key. The API key is associated with the session selected when it was created. The session UUID is also required when making a message request. Use the dashboard's Copy ID option to obtain it. 7. Sending Your First WhatsApp Message Through the REST API This is one of the most important parts of the project. Once the gateway is running and a WhatsApp session is connected, another application can send a text message using an authenticated HTTP request. API Endpoint POST /api/v1/messages/send Authentication Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Request Body { "sessionId" : "YOUR_SESSION_UUID" , "to" : "919876543210" , "type" : "text" , "message" : "Hello from Puffx WhatsApp Gateway!" } Replace the example phone number with the recipient's number, including the country code and digits only. Complete cURL Example curl -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/messages/send" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "sessionId": "YOUR_SESSION_UUID", "to": "919876543210", "type": "text", "message": "Hello from Puffx WhatsApp Gateway!" }' Replace the API key and session UUID with your actual values. The API returns HTTP 202 when the provider accepts the message request. An important distinction: HTTP 202 does not guarantee successful delivery or confirm that the recipient has read the message. Delivery and read receipts are not currently implemented in this beta. 8. Integrating with Other Programming Languages The gateway is designed to be accessed through HTTP, so a developer can integrate it with a backend written in different programming languages. Examples and integration guidance are included in the repository's API documentation. Potential client applications include: Node.js applications. PHP applications. Python applications. Internal business tools. Backend automation systems. For example, a PHP application could make an HTTP POST request to the gateway with its API key stored in a server-side environment variable. Never expose an API key in frontend JavaScript, a public GitHub repository, or a mobile application's publicly accessible configuration. For detailed examples, refer to: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/api-reference.md 9. Can It Run on a VPS? Yes. The application is designed for self-hosted deployment on a Linux VPS or cloud virtual machine. A typical deployment needs: Linux server. Docker Engine. Docker Compose. PostgreSQL. Persistent storage. Domain name. HTTPS reverse proxy. Outbound WebSocket connectivity. For public deployments, the gateway should run behind an HTTPS reverse proxy such as Nginx. The repository includes deployment documentation and an example Nginx configuration. A typical deployment workflow: Domain | v HTTPS Reverse Proxy | v Puffx WhatsApp Gateway | +------ PostgreSQL | +------ Persistent WhatsApp Session Data The Docker Compose configuration binds the gateway to localhost on port 3000. The reverse proxy forwards HTTPS requests to that local service. Ordinary shared hosting and static website hosting are generally unsuitable because the application requires continuously running services and persistent writable storage. For additional information: Docker deployment: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/docker-deployment.md VPS deployment: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/vps-deployment.md Installation guide: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/installation.md 10. Security Considerations Self-hosting gives developers control over their infrastructure, but it also means they are responsible for securing it. Some important considerations: Environment Secrets Use strong, unique secrets for the database password, session secret, and API key pepper. HTTPS Never expose a public dashboard or API over unencrypted HTTP. Configure a valid TLS certificate. API Key Protection Keep API keys in backend environment variables or a secret manager. Session Data WhatsApp authentication state is stored on disk and is not encrypted by the application. Protect the Docker volume and its backups. Database Backups Back up PostgreSQL and the WhatsApp authentication volume. Treat both as sensitive data. Access Restrictions Do not expose internal database ports or unnecessary services to the public internet. Read the full security documentation before deploying publicly: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/security.md 11. Current Beta Status and Limitations I want to be transparent about the current state of the project. Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is an initial beta implementation. Currently supported functionality: WhatsApp QR pairing. Phone pairing code. Web dashboard. Session management. API key creation. REST API authentication. Text message sending. Docker Compose deployment. Current limitations: Only text messages are supported. Media messaging is not implemented. Webhooks are not implemented. Message queues are not implemented. Delivery and read receipts are not implemented. There is no separate admin console. Real WhatsApp pairing and delivery behavior have not been verified by automated tests. These limitations are important. The project should not be treated as a fully production-ready messaging platform. 12. Why I Started This Project I enjoy exploring how software systems work beyond the frontend. Working on this project has given me an opportunity to explore: Backend architecture. REST API design. Database integration. Docker-based deployment. Authentication and secrets management. Persistent application data. VPS infrastructure. WhatsApp Web connectivity. I also wanted to build a practical tool that other developers could inspect, run, and experiment with. This is an ongoing learning and development project under Puffx Host. 13. Open Source and Community Feedback The project is publicly available on GitHub. I welcome feedback from developers who work with: Node.js. TypeScript. PostgreSQL. Docker. REST APIs. Backend development. Self-hosted infrastructure. You can explore the source code, read the documentation, report issues, and contribute improvements. GitHub Repository: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway If you find a bug or have a technical suggestion, please open an issue in the GitHub repository. Conclusion Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is my attempt to build a self-hosted messaging gateway with a practical REST API and Docker-based deployment. It is still in beta, and there is plenty of room for improvement. Building this project has been a useful experience in backend engineering, infrastructure, and API development. I would love to hear your feedback: What would you improve in a self-hosted WhatsApp messaging gateway? Would you focus on better session management, more API capabilities, monitoring, or deployment improvements? Explore the project: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway Built by Nitin Mehta | Puffx Host Website: https://puffxhost.com GitHub: https://github.com/puffxhost Disclaimer Puffx WhatsApp Gateway uses Baileys, an unofficial WhatsApp Web integration. It is not the official WhatsApp Business Platform and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by WhatsApp or Meta. WhatsApp pairing and service availability may change. Users are responsible for complying with applicable WhatsApp terms, local laws, privacy requirements, and recipient-consent requirements. Use this project responsibly.

title: Tired of uploading 40MB PNGs to your server and then slicing them (React + Canvas)
author: Krishna Kumar
summary: As a digital comic artists, we all know , we love exporting massive files. I run a small indie comic platform called ZealPlane and we were putting together chapters for our original series KARMA, G.O.D (unpublished) We’d often send over single vertical strips that were 1600px wide and 30,000px tall from Clip Studio Paint. even upto 45MB, just for a sinlge image. You obviously, can't serve a 30,000px tall PNG directly to a mobile browser unless you want your reader's phone to catch fire. Webtoons and Tapas make you chop up long vertical strips into 800x1280 pieces so they lazy-load cleanly as the user scrolls down. At first, Like many backend devs, I upload the file to a Node server, pipe it through sharp, zip up the slices, and send it back. turned out to be not a great idea. When you decode an uncompressed 1600x30000 RGBA image into memory on the server, it eats almost 200MB of raw RAM per request. It took was three or four people slicing chapters at the same time to spike our VPS memory and stall Nginx. Additionally, waiting 40 seconds just to upload a file on a slow connection and download the exact same pixels back felt super dumb. So a few weeks ago, I ripped out the backend endpoint and rewrote our Webtoon Slicer to run 100% in the browser. Zero uploads, zero server costs, and it finishes in like 300ms. Here are a few weird browser quirks I ran into while building it, in case anyone else is messing with huge images in React. Don't use FileReader.readAsDataURL() My first instinct was to read the uploaded file as a base64 string, stick it into an tag, and draw it onto a . Don't do this with 40MB files. Base64 inflates the string size by ~33%, and decoding a massive image on the main thread completely freezes the React UI for two seconds. Use createImageBitmap(file) instead. It takes the raw File or Blob directly from the file input and decodes it off the main thread. export async function sliceStrip(file, targetWidth = 800, sliceHeight = 1280) { // Decodes off-thread without base64 bloat const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(file); const scale = targetWidth / bitmap.width; const totalScaledHeight = Math.round(bitmap.height scale); const count = Math.ceil(totalScaledHeight / sliceHeight); const results = []; for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) { const currentY = i sliceHeight; const h = Math.min(sliceHeight, totalScaledHeight - currentY); // Map back to the original unscaled image coordinates const srcY = currentY / scale; const srcH = h / scale; const canvas = document.createElement('canvas'); canvas.width = targetWidth; canvas.height = h; const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d'); ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = true; ctx.imageSmoothingQuality = 'high'; ctx.drawImage( bitmap, 0, srcY, bitmap.width, srcH, 0, 0, targetWidth, h ); const blob = await new Promise((res) => canvas.toBlob(res, 'image/png')); results.push({ name: `slice_${String(i + 1).padStart(3, '0')}.png`, blob, url: URL.createObjectURL(blob), }); } // Crucial: free the GPU texture immediately! bitmap.close(); return results; } The 1px white line bug drove me crazy Once we got this working, our artists noticed something super annoying. On dark fantasy panels—especially stuff with heavy black/purple gradients like you see in Solo Leveling: Ragnarok's vertical fight scenes—there was occasionally a tiny 1-pixel horizontal grey seam where two sliced images met on mobile screens. Turns out, if an artist uploads an odd-width image (say 1240px wide) and you scale it down to 800px, srcY and srcH end up as floating-point decimals like 1984.3333px. When the HTML5 canvas samples sub-pixels along the very bottom edge of a crop, it blends the edge with empty transparent pixels, creating a faint semi-transparent border. Forcing integer math on the source crop coordinates (or keeping the artist's source canvas at an exact multiple like 1600px -> 800px) killed the seam lines immediately. Clean up your Object URLs or Safari will crash One thing you forget when working in a React SPA: URL.createObjectURL(blob) stays pinned in browser RAM until the document unloads or you manually revoke it. If an artist slices a 25-panel chapter, realizes they made a typo in a speech bubble, fixes it, and drops the file in again 4 times in a row, your tab is suddenly holding onto 100 uncompressed PNG blobs in memory. Mobile Safari will just hard-reload the tab without warning. Whenever the user resets the tool or drops a new file, loop through the old state first: useEffect(() => { return () => { slices.forEach((s) => URL.revokeObjectURL(s.url)); }; }, [slices]); And don't forget bitmap.close() at the end of your slicing function. Garbage collection on ImageBitmap is notoriously lazy in Chromium. Anyway, if you draw webcomics or just want to poke around with how it works in the browser, the tool is live here (no login or paywall or anything, it literally just runs in your tab): zealplane.com/tools/webtoon-slicer. How are you guys handling large client-side image jobs? Has anyone played around with OffscreenCanvas inside a Web Worker for this yet, or is standard createImageBitmap fast enough for your use cases? Sometimes a single image was 45MB. You obviously can't serve a 30,000px tall PNG directly to a mobile browser unless you want your reader's phone to catch fire. At first, I did what most backend devs do: upload the file to a Node server, pipe it through sharp , zip up the slices, and send it back. Bad idea. When you decode an uncompressed 1600x30000 RGBA image into memory on the server, it eats almost 200MB of raw RAM per request . All it took was three or four people slicing chapters at the same time to spike our VPS memory and stall Nginx. Plus, waiting 40 seconds just to upload a file on a slow connection and download the exact same pixels back felt super dumb. So a few weeks ago, I ripped out the backend endpoint and rewrote our zealplane.com/tools/webtoon-slicer to run 100% in the browser. Zero uploads, zero server costs, and it finishes in like 300ms. Here are a few weird browser quirks I ran into while building it, in case anyone else is messing with huge images in React. Don't use FileReader.readAsDataURL() My first instinct was to read the uploaded file as a base64 string, stick it into an tag, and draw it onto a . Don't do this with 40MB files. Base64 inflates the string size by ~33%, and decoding a massive image on the main thread completely freezes the React UI for two seconds. Use createImageBitmap(file) instead. It takes the raw File or Blob directly from the file input and decodes it off the main thread. export async function sliceStrip ( file , targetWidth = 800 , sliceHeight = 1280 ) { // Decodes off-thread without base64 bloat const bitmap = await createImageBitmap ( file ); const scale = targetWidth / bitmap . width ; const totalScaledHeight = Math . round ( bitmap . height * scale ); const count = Math . ceil ( totalScaledHeight / sliceHeight ); const results = []; for ( let i = 0 ; i < count ; i ++ ) { const currentY = i * sliceHeight ; const h = Math . min ( sliceHeight , totalScaledHeight - currentY ); // Map back to the original unscaled image coordinates const srcY = currentY / scale ; const srcH = h / scale ; const canvas = document . createElement ( ' canvas ' ); canvas . width = targetWidth ; canvas . height = h ; const ctx = canvas . getContext ( ' 2d ' ); ctx . imageSmoothingEnabled = true ; ctx . imageSmoothingQuality = ' high ' ; ctx . drawImage ( bitmap , 0 , srcY , bitmap . width , srcH , 0 , 0 , targetWidth , h ); const blob = await new Promise (( res ) => canvas . toBlob ( res , ' image/png ' )); results . push ({ name : `slice_ ${ String ( i + 1 ). padStart ( 3 , ' 0 ' )} .png` , blob , url : URL . createObjectURL ( blob ), }); } // Crucial: free the GPU texture immediately! bitmap . close (); return results ; } The 1px white line bug drove me crazy Once we got this working, our artists noticed something super annoying. On dark fantasy panels—especially stuff with heavy black/purple gradients like you see in Solo Leveling: Ragnarok's vertical fight scenes —there was occasionally a tiny 1-pixel horizontal grey seam where two sliced images met on mobile screens. Turns out, if an artist uploads an odd-width image (say 1240px wide) and you scale it down to 800px , srcY and srcH end up as floating-point decimals like 1984.3333px . When the HTML5 canvas samples sub-pixels along the very bottom edge of a crop, it blends the edge with empty transparent pixels, creating a faint semi-transparent border. Forcing integer math on the source crop coordinates (or keeping the artist's source canvas at an exact multiple like 1600px -> 800px ) killed the seam lines immediately. Clean up your Object URLs or Safari will crash One thing you forget when working in a React SPA: URL.createObjectURL(blob) stays pinned in browser RAM until the document unloads or you manually revoke it. If an artist slices a 25-panel chapter, realizes they made a typo in a speech bubble, fixes it, and drops the file in again 4 times in a row, your tab is suddenly holding onto 100 uncompressed PNG blobs in memory. Mobile Safari will just hard-reload the tab without warning. Whenever the user resets the tool or drops a new file, loop through the old state first: useEffect (() => { return () => { slices . forEach (( s ) => URL . revokeObjectURL ( s . url )); }; }, [ slices ]); And don't forget bitmap.close() at the end of your slicing function. Garbage collection on ImageBitmap is notoriously lazy in Chromium. Anyway, if you draw webcomics or just want to poke around with how it works in the browser, the tool is live here (no login or paywall or anything, it literally just runs in your tab): zealplane.com/tools/webtoon-slicer . How are you guys handling large client-side image jobs? Has anyone played around with OffscreenCanvas inside a Web Worker for this yet, or is standard createImageBitmap fast enough for your use cases?

title: Spark Radix vs Spark 2.3.1: What a 5M-Splat Desktop Test Shows
author: Alicia lu
summary: Originally published by Alicia on 31 October 2026 at Digital Garden . Original measurements and limitations are retained. AI-assisted disclosure: Codex helped construct the fixture, run the browser experiment, check the data and write this article. The measurements, excluded pilots, failures and untested boundaries are retained. I would keep Radix as a separate WebGPU experiment rather than migrate my garden for a speed claim. On October 31, 2026, I ran Radix 0.0.1 and Spark 2.3.1 on one Windows desktop with an RTX 5070 Ti. All three rendering paths stayed near the browser's 60 Hz presentation ceiling, including at five million source splats. That result cannot establish an unbounded speed ratio. The more useful difference was sorting: Radix's WebGL2 fallback continued presenting frames at about 60 FPS while its applied sort order updated less often. Its five-million-splat fast-orbit control measured about 58 ms from starting a sort to applying the result. I also checked the actual graphics calls, format failures, opaque/transparent mesh integration and one raycast interaction. Actual browser capture, not a photographic scan. Fixture and figures by Alicia, CC BY 4.0. What I actually tested This is an isolated integration study for Digital Garden , not a replacement of its live renderer. The asset is an owned, deterministic synthetic flower-bed stress fixture , with 36 green beds and pink, yellow and purple flower shapes. It is not a photographic garden capture. SH degree is zero, so it cannot test higher-order view-dependent appearance. The same SPZ v3 file at each size reached every renderer: 500,000 / 2,000,000 / 5,000,000 splats, about 6.44 / 25.76 / 64.39 MB. A normal opaque Three.js cube shares the scene. I checked the decoded counts rather than accepting an empty canvas's FPS. Component Tested setting Workstation Ryzen 9 9950X, approximately 64 GiB RAM, RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, driver 617.42 OS and browser Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26300, embedded Chrome 156.0.0.0 Libraries Three.js 0.186.1, Radix 0.0.1, Spark 2.3.1 Canvas 1920 × 1080 drawing buffer, renderer pixel ratio 1, antialias off Radix paths Explicit WebGPU and explicit webgpu-gl; active backend checked Spark path WebGLRenderer / WebGL2, dynamic LoD disabled Shots Fixed camera and one identical orbit per 15 seconds Repetitions Discard 5 seconds of warmup, then three 15-second measurements per configuration That makes 54 accepted trials, 810 measured seconds and 48,597 recorded RAF intervals. No trial became hidden. The machine retained its normal desktop environment, with incidental editorial work; this was not an exclusive thermal or device-isolation test. The order was fixed, not randomized. I changed one Radix integration setting before freezing the measured harness: directCanvas:false . With the default direct canvas path, the ordinary MeshBasicMaterial and clear color differed in my pilot. Using Three.js's output path aligned the ordinary scene's color handling. That adds an output pass, so this is not a reproduction of the official default-settings benchmark. Both renderers use radial sorting here. Radix uses its default EWA projection and 24-bit sort. I did not tune all footprint/culling parameters to prove equal image quality. Matching asset, camera and resolution is necessary, but it does not by itself make two rasterizers equivalent. The FPS result has a ceiling The orbit results below pool the raw samples from three repetitions. RAF is the time between browser animation callbacks. CPU time wraps the synchronous renderer.render call and excludes work on a worker and GPU completion. Source splats Path RAF mean / p95 ms CPU mean / p95 ms Hitches > 2× median 0.5M Radix WebGPU 16.67 / 16.80 0.271 / 0.400 0 0.5M Radix WebGL2 16.67 / 16.80 0.816 / 1.100 0 0.5M Spark 2.3.1 WebGL2 16.67 / 16.80 0.154 / 0.300 0 2M Radix WebGPU 16.67 / 16.80 0.280 / 0.400 0 2M Radix WebGL2 16.67 / 16.80 0.860 / 1.600 0 2M Spark 2.3.1 WebGL2 16.67 / 16.80 0.219 / 0.300 1 5M Radix WebGPU 16.67 / 16.80 0.355 / 0.500 0 5M Radix WebGL2 16.67 / 16.80 0.677 / 1.700 0 5M Spark 2.3.1 WebGL2 16.67 / 16.80 0.221 / 0.400 0 All the orbit p95 values round to 16.80 ms. The full suite retained two intervals above the strict hitch threshold, including a 33.4 ms fixed-shot Radix WebGPU interval at five million splats. Those outliers remain in the report; I did not remove them to improve the graph. The CPU call costs differ, but none is a complete renderer cost. A shorter Spark main-thread call does not count its worker's sorting time. Likewise, WebGPU dispatch submission can return before GPU execution. I would not turn these columns into a headline “x times faster” comparison. Separate timestamp diagnostics add context. At five million splats during the orbit, Radix WebGPU reported mean projection / sort / draw phases of about 0.36 / 1.33 / 7.14 ms. Spark's separate WebGL render query averaged about 5.94 ms. These probes use different backend-specific timing paths and do not include the same asynchronous work. The Radix draw phase also includes the normal scene/output work. They are useful receipts, not a matched total-latency ranking. A 60 FPS fallback can still show an older order Radix's sorting documentation distinguishes the same-frame GPU sort from the WebGL2 key pass, readback and worker sort. I checked worker messages and successive applied-order versions in my run. Source splats Applied-order interval mean / p95 ms Worker round-trip mean / p95 ms Key pass + readback mean / p95 ms 0.5M 16.68 / 16.80 2.78 / 5.90 4.78 / 6.30 2M 33.40 / 33.40 11.74 / 13.10 10.53 / 13.50 5M 55.45 / 66.70 27.29 / 29.20 21.70 / 29.60 The stationary shot can reuse an order. The moving camera produces new ones, but the five-million-splat fallback did not deliver a new order every presented frame. Its roughly 55 ms order interval and 16.67 ms RAF interval describe different parts of the pipeline. I then recorded a separate six-second fast orbit: two turns, three seconds per turn, at five million splats. Wrapping the view's public sort/apply methods measured 89 completed Radix WebGL2 sorts. Start-to-apply delay averaged 57.88 ms , with 64.30 ms p95 and 79.90 ms maximum . The camera moved an average 0.87 world units between those two events. The three clips are 1080p VP9 at about 15 fps and fully decoded with ffmpeg. Recording overhead is included in that control and excluded from the main comparison. The flower-bed fixture stayed recognizable in the inspected frames. I did not measure a flicker rate or establish that photographic edges and transparent foliage would look acceptable. One splat draw is real, and Spark does it too I captured application calls to the graphics APIs after settling the scene, using one and then three objects with 500,000 splats each. Radix WebGPU issued one drawIndexedIndirect for the combined splat collection in both cases. Three objects added three projection dispatches, but not three splat draws. Radix WebGL2 similarly issued one instanced splat draw. Spark also issued one drawElementsInstanced for the combined 500,000 / 1,500,000 splats. Therefore batching overlapping objects is useful, but this control does not establish it as a Radix-only advantage. Whole-scene draw totals were 3 for Radix WebGPU and 2 for Spark: cube, splats and, for the controlled Radix path, the output pass. Radix WebGL2 added fragment passes and reported 7 / 8 calls in these captures. “One splat draw” does not mean “one call for the entire application.” These are API-boundary captures, not a Spector.js or complete hardware trace. Format and integration checks changed the migration question SPZ v3 worked throughout the measured matrix. Additional 500,000-splat files were written from the same source data: Format Radix 0.0.1 WebGPU Spark 2.3.1 WebGL2 PLY 500,000 decoded and drawn 500,000 decoded and drawn SPZ v4 500,000 decoded and drawn Failed: Invalid gzip header RDX 500,000 decoded and drawn Failed: Unknown file type Those failures belong to the pinned versions and files. I did not separately exercise SPLAT, KSPLAT, compressed PLY, RAD or the SOG/LCC example adapters. Core formats and example importers should not be conflated. The opaque cube rendered with the expected front/back occlusion in all three paths. A transparent cube with opacity 0.45 and depthWrite=false also rendered, but its composition differed. Sorting all Gaussian objects together does not promise exact interleaving with arbitrary transparent Three.js meshes. The stills are similar rather than pixel-identical. The five-million-splat Radix/Spark comparison had approximately 1.25/255 whole-image RGB mean absolute error, or 4.07/255 over the foreground union. This is a descriptive difference; the large shared background must not be mistaken for a quality pass. A central Three.js Raycaster ray hit the ordinary cube on every path. It returned four Spark splat hits and zero Radix splat hits in this setup. Radix offers CPU-picking examples, but I did not port one. A working render is not a drop-in replacement for Spark's per-Gaussian picking API. Installation and teardown belong in the result A normal Windows npm installation of Radix 0.0.1 failed with EBADPLATFORM: the published package required macOS-only fsevents. I used npm pack with scripts disabled, retained the official tarball integrity, and imported its unchanged prebuilt modules. The runtime then worked on both backends. This is a package-install workaround, not a rendering speed optimization. The harness also exposed a Spark teardown boundary. Disposing while asynchronous sorting was active produced unhandled Promise events; a focused transition control reproduced four, including a readbackDepth / driveSort “No target” stack. I kept those failures and added a separately verified quiesce-before-dispose runner. The accepted timing data and frozen original harness remain intact. The workaround uses exposed fields of pinned Spark 2.3.1 and needs rechecking for another version. Would I switch the garden? I would continue evaluating Radix for a bounded WebGPU scene that benefits from compute sorting or TSL-generated splats. I would keep Spark where its existing LoD/paging, asset handling and picking workflow are needed. Radix's public examples implement some features outside the core, so a simplistic “Radix cannot do edits or picking” table would hide possible integration work. For my garden, these 54 trials do not justify a migration for FPS. The next useful study would use a licensed photographic scene with nonzero SH, matched visual controls, a scene that actually exceeds the display budget, and the target devices. Phones, Safari, Firefox, headsets, higher-order SH, 10M splats, streaming, sustained thermals and production integration remain untested. The official Radix benchmark remains evidence from its own machine, scenes and settings. Its live report now discusses matched culling and frame stalls in detail. I have not copied an older draft's Apple M3 speed ratio into my results. For the earlier integration route, see Spark vs GaussianSplats3D vs Native Three.js , Gaussian splats in Three.js and the Spirula garden sample . Those published experiments are separate from this synthetic Radix study. Download the reproducible study Reproduction ZIP · Size and SHA-256 · Raw-derived results JSON · CSV · Integration controls · Fixture hashes · Environment · Full test report . The 12,002,053-byte ZIP contains 160 files: the pinned harness and official package modules, all accepted raw timing and GPU observations, API/format/picking/lifecycle receipts, selected figures, three recordings and the 0.5M SPZ. Regenerate the omitted 2M/5M and additional-format fixture binaries with the included generator. Original image/recording-data JSON and most full-resolution captures remain local. The pinned Radix source maps are omitted; they can produce an optional Vite debug warning. The unpacked package passed dependency installation, build, hash verification and a three-path browser pilot. The safe runner waits for Spark 2.3.1 sorting before teardown; the frozen measured runner and its original failures are retained. Read the environment and test report before interpreting a rerun.
