title: How to Turn Your Lyrics into a Song with AI
author: SoundLuma
summary: By SoundLuma editorial team To turn lyrics into a song with AI, prepare clean lyric text, separate it into sections, and choose a service that accepts custom lyrics. Then describe the arrangement independently, generate a version, and check the words and melody together. A text-to-music prompt and a custom-lyrics field may behave differently, so check which input mode you are using. If you already have verses, you can organize them in the SoundLuma lyrics workspace . For enabled trial accounts, choose My lyrics → song in the generator, enter your lyrics, title, and music style, then generate. The optional brief workspace farther down the page exports text only. If you have a memory rather than lyrics, start with the story-to-song method . Key takeaways Put only the words you want sung in the lyric field. Keep section labels consistent and arrangement instructions separate. Review pronunciation, missing lines, and section order in every generated version. Prepare a readable lyric sheet Remove notes such as “rewrite this later,” duplicate drafts, and comments intended for a collaborator. Decide which chorus version is final. A model cannot reliably know that the crossed-out line in your working document is not part of the song. Use blank lines between sections. Simple labels such as [Verse 1], [Chorus], and [Bridge] can make your intention clear to a human reader, but support varies by music service. If the service documents another format, follow it. Bracketed text is not a universal command language and may sometimes be sung. Here is an original fictional example: [Verse 1] We counted windows on the train And drew our names against the rain [Chorus] Wherever all these miles may go You're still the place I know The example is a starting pattern, not a claim about how any particular model will perform it. Read each section out loud Look for a line that takes much longer to say than its neighbors. It may still work musically, but it deserves attention before you spend a generation attempt. Replace a crowded sentence with a simpler phrase while keeping its meaning. For example, “I appreciate how you consistently supported me when everything was changing” might become “You stayed when everything changed.” You lose detail, so decide whether another verse should show what that support looked like. The goal is to make space for expression rather than force every thought into one line. Do not change a meaningful word just to obtain a rhyme. If the rhyme makes your message less accurate, leave it open or change both lines. Write a separate arrangement brief Describe instrumentation, vocal character, mood, and energy. A useful brief could be: “Piano-led ballad, intimate female vocal, restrained first verse, a fuller final chorus, clear words, short ending.” This gives direction without promising a specific output. Choose the language of the actual lyrics. If you mix languages, mark the intended transitions in a way your chosen service supports. Do not assume a language dropdown will translate your text while preserving rhyme or meaning. For a birthday track, an energetic arrangement may suit the party, while a quieter arrangement may suit a personal message. Choose one shared memory and one wish for the year ahead so the song stays personal. Turn your lyrics into audio in SoundLuma Open the AI song generator and sign in with Google. Audio generation is currently a limited trial for enabled accounts; signing in alone does not guarantee access or an available attempt. Select My lyrics → song . The ordinary song mode asks for an idea and generates lyrics automatically; instrumental mode makes music without vocals. Enter your lyric sheet, a title, and a separate music style. The current form accepts up to 5,000 characters of lyrics, an 80-character title, and a 200-character style description. Use Chinese, English, or mixed-language lyrics as intended. You do not need to translate your words into English to submit them. Submit once and follow the progress. If the site says the submission result is pending confirmation, check your history and contact support instead of submitting it again. Listen to every returned track. A generation can return more than one version; keep the version that best delivers your words and download it before its displayed expiry date. On October 21, 2026, our production integration test completed a custom-lyrics task and returned two tracks. That verifies submission and result retrieval, not perfect pronunciation or faithful performance of every line. Your listening check still matters. Generated tracks start private. Publishing to the audio gallery is a separate, optional action that lets other people listen and download. Check the sharing confirmation before publishing personal lyrics or stories. Handle names and pronunciation deliberately Names, initials, and unusual place names need a dedicated listening check. A spelling that looks correct may be sung differently from what you expect. If the service allows phonetic guidance, use its documented method. Otherwise, consider a nickname the recipient actually uses. Keep a written lyric sheet with the correct spelling even if you use a pronunciation aid during generation. Listen to the whole line after changing a name; a fix can alter its rhythm. Compare versions with a short checklist Check whether every intended section appears, whether a line is repeated unexpectedly, and whether the key message remains understandable. Listen for truncated endings and words that are stretched beyond recognition. Compare versions using the same checks so you are choosing deliberately rather than following whichever chorus you heard last. If a verse is crowded, edit the verse before asking for more versions. If the performance feels wrong but the words work, change the arrangement description. Change one kind of input at a time when you want to understand what helped. Can you use any lyrics you find online? Use lyrics you wrote or have permission to use. Access to a lyric website does not establish permission to reproduce those words in a new recording. Commercial release also depends on your chosen service's current terms and any rights in the material you supply; a download button alone does not settle that question. Save your final lyric sheet and style brief together. That gives you a clear reference for revisions and a useful starting point if you try another arrangement later.

title: How to Turn a Story into a Song
author: SoundLuma
summary: By SoundLuma editorial team To turn a story into a song, choose one meaningful moment, describe what changed, and build a chorus around the feeling you want to leave behind. A song does not need every event in the story. It needs enough recognizable detail for the listener to feel why the moment matters. This guide uses an original fictional example: two friends miss the last bus after moving to a new city. One shares a blue umbrella. That ordinary evening becomes a story about finding belonging. You can prepare the same kind of brief in the SoundLuma song workspace , where the optional story workspace prepares a text brief. The generator above it offers audio generation for enabled trial accounts. Key takeaways Pick one scene and one emotional change before choosing a music style. Keep names, places, and concrete details that the recipient will recognize. Review lyrics before making music; a factual error can survive into every chorus. Start with a moment, not a biography Write a paragraph answering four questions: Who is the song for? Where were you? What happened? Why does it matter now? Use your normal speaking voice. You can edit the wording later. For example: “Sam and I had just moved to the city. We missed the last bus after our first week at college. Sam shared a blue umbrella and made me laugh all the way home. I want this song to thank them for making the city feel less lonely.” That paragraph contains a setting, an action, a recognizable object, and a reason to sing. A list of every school, job, and holiday would offer more information but less direction. If you need several memories, choose one as the opening scene and save the others for later verses. Separate the story from its message The event is missing the bus. The message is “you made a strange place feel like home.” Put the message in a short sentence before attempting rhyme. That sentence is your chorus brief. A useful planning map is: verse one shows the unfamiliar city; the chorus thanks the friend; verse two shows how the friendship continued; the final chorus returns to the same central thought. This is a writing option, not a mandatory song structure. A short dedication might need only one verse and a chorus. Turn details into singable lines Move from explanation to a scene the listener can picture. Instead of “you were a supportive friend during a difficult transition,” try “you held the blue umbrella wide.” The second line gives the singer an action and the listener an image. Original draft lines might read: We watched the last bus disappear You held the blue umbrella near A city full of streets unknown You laughed, and it began to feel like home These are illustrative lyrics, not the transcript of a generated song. Keep any line that sounds like you, and rewrite details that do not fit your experience. See the lyrics preparation guide for section labels and a revision checklist. Add musical direction without burying the story Give the music service a separate style description: “Warm acoustic pop, conversational vocal, gentle guitar, hopeful chorus, no long instrumental opening.” Keep production instructions out of the lyric lines unless your chosen service documents a specific instruction format. Choose a mood that suits the recipient. An upbeat reunion song and a quiet thank-you can use the same memory but need different arrangements. You do not need to name a famous singer to describe warmth, tempo, instrumentation, or vocal energy. Review the words before generating audio Check names, dates, pronouns, and who did what. Read the lyric aloud and listen for sentences that need too much explanation. A chorus should still make sense if someone hears it without the verses. Ask whether any detail is too private to share. A song for one friend may include a joke that would be uncomfortable on a public gift page. Keep a private version and a public version if necessary; do not assume that uploading a story automatically makes it suitable for publishing. What should you do if the story feels too long? Keep one scene, one object, and one message. Save the full prose as background material, then write a shorter lyric brief. For a relationship story, the love song guide shows how to connect an early memory to a present-day promise. For a friend, use the friendship song prompts . When the brief reads clearly, choose a music service that supports your intended input and review its current generation and download options. SoundLuma's optional workspace can organize and export your text brief. Enabled trial accounts can use the generator above it to describe a song or turn their own lyrics into audio.

title: An API that misses its deadline should pay you back: a bonded pay-per-call escrow on Arc
author: Edy Cu
summary: Your agent paid an API 0.01 USDC and the API never answered. Unless the provider decides to refund you, that money is gone, and your only recourse is a refund policy, a support ticket or a chargeback. The provider had nothing at stake. I wanted the opposite default: if the API misses its deadline, it pays you back, plus a penalty, without you having to ask. ReplyBond is a small Solidity escrow on Arc mainnet that does exactly that, and this post walks through the five design choices that make it work, what the AI coding agent (Arc Studio) built, what I did by hand, and where it stops being honest to call it "guaranteed". Live: https://replybond.edycu.dev (Arc mainnet, chain 5042, native USDC) Repo: https://github.com/edycutjong/replybond (MIT) Contract: 0x2a0f4aeF8E5379d8E4606F40846cf97716fe749f , Sourcify exact match Job 24 on mainnet: the provider stays silent, the 45 s clock (sped up x8) hits zero, timeout pays the buyer 0.010 back + 0.005 from the bond, and the explorer shows the same transaction moving 0.015 USDC. The shape of a job A provider posts an offer with a bond. A buyer accepts it by paying the price, and the clock starts on acceptance. Every job ends in exactly one of four terminal states: Ending Who triggers it Who gets price + bond Paid buyer calls acknowledge after an answer provider Claimed anyone calls claim after the answer + a grace window provider TimedOut anyone calls timeout after the deadline, no answer buyer Withdrawn provider withdraws an offer nobody took provider (bond only) There is no owner and no upgrade path. On the demo, the price is 0.010 USDC, the bond 0.005 USDC, the response window 45 s and the grace window 120 s. 1. The bond goes in before the buyer pays The order matters. The provider locks the penalty first, as msg.value on postOffer ; only then can a buyer accept by paying exactly price : function postOffer( bytes32 requestHash, address buyer, uint256 price, uint64 responseWindow, uint64 graceWindow ) external payable nonReentrant returns (uint256 id) { if (msg.value == 0) revert InvalidBond(); if (price == 0) revert InvalidPrice(); if (responseWindow == 0) revert InvalidResponseWindow(); ... Because USDC is Arc's native balance, the bond, the price, the penalty and the gas are all the same asset. There are no ERC-20 approvals in the flow at all: one payable call locks the bond, another locks the price. 2. "Answering" means writing the output on-chain A deadline is meaningless if "I answered" is just the provider's word. So an answer only counts if the provider calls respond with the output itself, between 1 and 1,024 bytes, at or before the deadline: function respond(uint256 id, bytes calldata output) external nonReentrant { Job storage job = _requireJob(id); if (msg.sender != job.provider) revert NotProvider(id); _requireStatus(id, job, Status.Accepted); if (block.timestamp > uint256(job.deadline)) revert ResponseDeadlinePassed(id); if (output.length == 0 || output.length > MAX_OUTPUT) revert InvalidOutputLength(output.length); job.responseHash = keccak256(output); job.respondedAt = uint64(block.timestamp); job.status = Status.Responded; emit ResponseCommitted(id, job.responseHash, output, job.respondedAt); } The contract stores only the keccak256 and emits the bytes in the ResponseCommitted event, so delivery is provable from the chain alone, and MAX_OUTPUT bounds the gas. The boundary is deliberate: respond is valid up to and including the deadline, timeout only strictly after it, so there is no second where both are possible. 3. Nobody has to ask for the refund timeout is permissionless. Anyone can call it once the deadline passes, and the money always goes to the buyer, never to the caller: function timeout(uint256 id) external nonReentrant { Job storage job = _requireJob(id); _requireStatus(id, job, Status.Accepted); if (block.timestamp <= uint256(job.deadline)) revert DeadlineNotPassed(id); uint256 amount = job.price + job.bond; job.status = Status.TimedOut; emit JobTimedOut(id, job.buyer, msg.sender, amount); _pay(id, job.buyer, amount); } The mirror case needed the same treatment. If the provider did answer and the buyer simply goes quiet, the provider must not be stuck: after respondedAt + graceWindow , anyone can call claim , and the provider gets price + bond. A silent buyer cannot take the answer and keep the money. 4. A payout must never block another job Pushing native value to an arbitrary address is the classic way to brick an escrow: one payee that reverts (or burns gas, or returns a huge blob) and settlement is stuck. ReplyBond sends with a 100,000-gas cap and a zero-length return area, so it never copies return data: function _pay(uint256 id, address payee, uint256 amount) internal { totalLocked -= amount; if (!_sendNative(payee, amount)) { owed[payee] += amount; totalOwed += amount; emit PayoutOwed(id, payee, amount); } } /// @dev Bounded gas and zero-length return area: never copies returndata. function _sendNative(address payee, uint256 amount) private returns (bool success) { assembly ("memory-safe") { success := call(PAYOUT_GAS, payee, amount, 0, 0, 0, 0) } } If the send fails, the amount is credited to owed[payee] and the payee pulls it later with withdrawOwed() . State changes happen before any payout, and every entry point sits behind OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard . The contract's doc comment writes down the invariants the Foundry suite checks, including conservation (balance >= totalLocked + totalOwed ) and "each job reaches exactly one terminal state, once". 5. Read the payout from the chain's own Transfer log This is the part only Arc gives you, and the one I liked most. On Arc, a native USDC movement out of a contract shows up in the receipt as an ERC-20-style Transfer log emitted by a system address (EIP-7708), right next to the contract's own events. From a real testnet timeout receipt: log#25 emitter=0x1234fb0f...2458 [ReplyBond] JobTimedOut(id=1, amount=15000000000000000) log#26 emitter=0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe [ARC SYSTEM EMITTER] Transfer(from=<contract>, to=<buyer>, value=15000000000000000) So the app does not trust its own contract's event to say "paid". classifyReceipt only returns PAID when the receipt carries the settle event and a system-emitter Transfer from the contract to that payee for that exact amount: export const SYSTEM_EMITTER = ' 0xffffFFFfFFffffffffffffffFfFFFfffFFFfFFfE ' const TRANSFER_TOPIC = ' 0xddf252ad1be2c89b69c2b068fc378daa952ba7f163c4a11628f55a4df523b3ef ' const transfer = receipt . logs . find ( ( l ) => l . address . toLowerCase () === SYSTEM_EMITTER . toLowerCase () && l . topics . length === 3 && l . topics [ 0 ]. toLowerCase () === TRANSFER_TOPIC && topicAddress ( l . topics [ 1 ]) === contract . toLowerCase () && topicAddress ( l . topics [ 2 ]) === settle . payee . toLowerCase () && BigInt ( l . data as Hex ) === settle . amount , ) if ( ! transfer ) return none ( ' no USDC Transfer log to the payee ' , base ) The UI stamps "INDEMNITY PAID" only on a PAID result. One bug here is worth naming: an early version stored a rate-limited RPC read as a permanent failure. Unreadable receipts now retry with backoff instead of being recorded as unreadable for good. What the AI agent built, and what I did by hand The contract, its Foundry tests, the API routes and the React app came from Arc Studio turns, driven with the Studio CLI ( arc-studio run / pull ) and committed in order; each commit subject names its turn. Studio wrote the contract in turn 1, deployed it to Arc testnet and ran the Foundry suite there. Later turns built the app, the demo-provider and demo-buyer routes, the receipt classifier, and fixes such as Vercel's file tracer folding BigInt math on a null binding and breaking the build. What Studio did not do: mainnet. Studio deploys to testnet only, so I deployed the unchanged Studio source with forge create from my own keystore. contracts/ReplyBond.sol has not changed since Studio turn 1, and Sourcify reports an exact match, which is the check that the bytecode on mainnet really is that source. The numbers: forge test on the pinned forge 1.7.1 gives 66 passed, 0 failed (63 unit and fuzz tests plus 3 invariants at 256 runs); bun test tests/ gives 116 passed, 0 failed across 16 files. One run through the live app on mainnet covered all three settlement paths, each moving 0.015 USDC: acknowledge , timeout and claim . Where it stops being a guarantee Delivery, not correctness. The contract proves an output was delivered on-chain on time. It does not prove the output is right. Outputs are public and capped at 1,024 bytes. The demo provider is an echo service. It answers with your input in capitals, so the demo proves timing and payment, not useful answers. Permissionless is not automatic. Someone has to send timeout or claim . The server does it for demo jobs. No always-on worker. The demo provider answers only while some request runs the sweep (a page load, an API call, or the daily cron). A buyer who accepts a job and never calls the API can time it out and collect the bond. That is the timeout path working as designed against a provider that is not always on, and the demo bounds it with 20 new offers per hour, 80 per day and a 0.1 USDC wallet floor. Unaudited , and the demo fixes price, bond and windows rather than letting the buyer choose them per call. Next on the list: an always-on provider worker, per-call deadlines and bonds, and a way to check answers so that correctness, not only delivery, can back a payout. title: hotellobby (LobbyDuo): UX Notes on Preview-Before-Pay AI Booth Videos
author: Hotel Lobby Lab
summary: How I shipped a two-photo → Hotel Lobby booth duo on Cloudflare Workers — optimizing framing preview before Stripe, with Seedance via TryAllAPI. Trend video products usually fail at the same moment: the user pays, then discovers their faces are cropped wrong. For tryhotellobby.app (product name hotellobby / LobbyDuo ) I optimized the UX before the charge , not another prompt textarea. Upload two adult face photos → ~15s orange COLORS-style booth duo (9:16 / 16:9 / 21:9, 480p or 720p) with original/AI booth audio. Independent tool — not affiliated with any artist group. This post is the builder + UX walkthrough. Prices and model ids change; treat live site / console as source of truth. UX thesis: preview framing, then unlock Create The homepage copy is blunt: free scene preview before you pay — upload two photos, check framing in the orange booth layout, then unlock Create with a one-time pack. That sequence matters more than fancy motion poetry: Photo 1 → left of the booth duo. Photo 2 → right . Local/layout preview of how faces sit in the booth. Only then: Stripe → credits → Seedance render. Users who can see “my face is too small / off-center” before paying convert better and refund less. Free-form “make a hotel video” prompts do the opposite: ambiguity first, charge second, regret third. Live packs verified on-site while writing: Single $8.88 (≈ 500 credits / one 720p), 3-pack $16.99 , plus larger packs (and occasional cheaper 480p messaging). Guest Stripe — no account for a single video. Always re-check the create CTA before you screenshot a price for a friend. Why left/right roles beat a single “upload faces” dump Booth memes are spatial. If the UI does not say who stands where, users invent their own convention and then complain the sample “looks different.” Fixed seats: Remove “who is who?” support tickets. Stabilize the locked template prompt sent upstream. Make demos honest — the sample matches the seats. Aspect ratio is a first-class control (9:16 default for Reels/TikTok; 16:9 / 21:9 for other cuts). Original/AI booth audio means the download is shareable without hunting a track. Stack overview Layer Choice Role Front / SSR TanStack Start (Vite) Landing, upload panel, generation status Runtime Cloudflare Workers Edge deploy, secrets, API routes DB Cloudflare D1 Credits, orders, task rows (table prefixes if DBs are shared) Payments Stripe Checkout One-time packs + optional larger packs; guest checkout Video upstream TryAllAPI → Seedance Async create + poll Analytics GA Funnel sanity check two faces → booth layout preview → check credits (else Stripe) → Worker creates Seedance task via TryAllAPI → poll until MP4 URL → store / show → on failure: refund credits Demo clips are self-hosted. Do not hotlink someone else’s sample MP4 for marketing. Why a video API aggregator Operational checklist after register / top-up: Confirm available USD balance in the console (not only the checkout success page). Create a token in pay-as-you-go style billing. Enable the video / Seedance-related channel group on that token. Wrong group → “no available channel” even when the model id looks right. Prefer separate keys per product ( hotellobby-prod vs sandbox). Put the key only in Workers Secrets (for example TRYALLAPI_API_KEY ). Never in the frontend bundle or a blog post. Conceptually the call shape looks like this (field names follow the aggregator’s v3 contents API; always re-check current docs): POST /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks Authorization: Bearer <TRYALLAPI_API_KEY> Content-Type: application/json Accept-Encoding: identity GET /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks/{id} I send Accept-Encoding: identity from the Worker because some gateways behave badly with transparent decompression. Model ids used in production look like Seedance 2.x family strings — treat console ids as source of truth, not this paragraph. Seedance parameters that matter for booth duos A few details that bit me across this family of sites: Pass duration as an explicit integer. Some models default to “smart length.” Omitting duration can silently lengthen the clip and the bill. resolution and ratio . Cost tracks resolution tier and duration more than portrait vs landscape. Match whatever the create UI offers (often 480p/720p and 9:16 for Shorts). generate_audio . When the product ships “finished” downloads, leave audio on; creators who want a trending sound can mute later. Status machine. Expect something like queued → running → succeeded / failed . Success URLs are often short-lived signed links — download/rehost on your side before handing the file to the user. Decent failure. On supply_unavailable or hard failures: refund credits, show a short human message, log the detailed upstream error server-side, optionally fall back to another Seedance tier. Rough mental model for upstream cost (illustrative only — use your own usage fields and invoices): tokens ≈ duration_sec × width × height × fps / 1024 cost ≈ tokens × price_per_million_tokens Price the site after you measure a few real 720p runs with retry margin, Stripe fees, and failed-job refunds — not from a spreadsheet fantasy of 0% failure. Booth-specific: map two reference images to left/right seats consistently; same-person clones in both seats look wrong — the UI should say so. Credits, Stripe, and guest checkout Demo UIs are easy. The line between toy and product is: User hits Create → check credit balance. If short → Stripe Checkout Session (guest allowed). Webhook (plus a return-URL sync check) grants credits. Pre-debit / lock credits, create upstream task, persist task_id in D1. Poll until done; succeed → show MP4; fail → refund credits . Two books of account stay separate: USD balance at TryAllAPI (your cost) vs site credits (what you sold). Mixing them in one mental ledger is how you underprice or invent “mysterious” losses. When several products share one Stripe account, isolate webhooks by endpoint or by metadata ( site / product ). Callbacks pointed at the wrong apex domain are a classic multi-site footgun. Secrets stay in Workers: TRYALLAPI_API_KEY , STRIPE_SECRET_KEY , webhook secret, auth secrets. The browser only ever sees publishable Stripe keys if needed. Deploy notes (Workers + D1) Typical loop on this template family: pnpm install # wire D1 database_id, production env, custom domain in wrangler pnpm cf:deploy Before calling a deploy “done”: D1 binding is correct; shared DBs use table prefixes , not a new database per micro-idea (free-tier DB counts are limited). AUTH_TRUSTED_ORIGINS and Stripe return / webhook URLs match the production HTTPS origin. GA id is set for a coarse funnel (land → upload → pay → wait → download). One real end-to-end path on production or a staging Worker: upload → pay → render → download. Production origin for Checkout / auth trust: https://tryhotellobby.app (alternate brand hostnames may exist — keep allowlists in sync with the URL users actually pay on). Product rules that are not optional Face-based generation is not “just another SaaS CRUD app”: Require an explicit 18+ / rights-to-use confirmation on upload. Block minors and refuse celebrity / stranger misuse in copy and policy. Expect upstream safety refusals; refund and explain. Keep privacy policy honest about retention; do not train on user media by default. Market as an independent fan-style tool for a trend format — not as an official tie-in unless you actually have that deal. Use your own sample renders in marketing. Those constraints belong in the product, not in a footnote you add after the first dispute email. What the UX taught me Preview-before-pay reduces “bad crop” chargebacks more than shaving another dollar off the Single pack. Locked booth layout beats free-form hotel prompts. Guest Single pack (~$8.88) matches “I need one clip tonight.” Credits with automatic refund on failed generation is table stakes. Measure land → upload → pay → wait → download before rewriting marketing adjectives. Consumer path: tryhotellobby.app — watch the sample, upload two authorized adult faces, preview framing, pay once. Builder path: TryAllAPI , top up, prove create+poll, then polish the preview UX. Sell confidence in framing first; sell GPU second.
